 Infiltration Wells and the Importance of Groundwater Recharge
 Parts of Indonesia have entered the rainy season. As flood risks rise, infiltration wells help reduce runoff while replenishing groundwater.
 Floods Aren’t Just Rainfall Infiltration Wells Reduce Runoff The rainy season has returned. The scent of wet earth is starting to be felt after rain drenched several cities in Indonesia. The Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) predicts the start of the 2026 rainy season will arrive gradually in November and December across most regions, peaking through February 2027. 
 News of floods has become a near-regular fixture of every rainy season. Jakarta, Bekasi, Semarang, and several other cities have repeatedly been hit by inundation when heavy rain falls. 
 In the previous rainy season, major floods also struck various parts of Java and Sumatra, disrupting people’s activities and forcing thousands of residents to evacuate. 
 That condition is often seen as a consequence of high rainfall intensity. Yet according to Drs. Yuli Priyana, M.Si., a lecturer at the Faculty of Geography , Universitas Muhammadiyah Surakarta (UMS), rain is not the only cause of flooding. 
 “The main problem actually lies in the disruption of the hydrological cycle because the soil’s ability to absorb water keeps shrinking,” said the UMS climatology expert, Friday (13/11/2026). 
 Floods Aren’t Just Rainfall
 Yuli’s observations said that in recent decades many green open spaces have slowly turned into residential areas, paved roads, and concrete buildings. Surfaces that once absorbed water have become waterproof layers. 
 As a result, most rainwater flows straight over the surface to drains and rivers within a short time. This is one cause of floods that are becoming more frequent in urban areas. 
 Yuli explained that under natural conditions about 50 percent of rainwater soaks into the ground as infiltration, while the rest returns to the atmosphere through evapotranspiration or flows off as surface runoff. But when land is covered with concrete and asphalt, infiltration capacity drops sharply. In fact, 80 to 90 percent of rainwater can turn directly into surface runoff. 
 “The water arrives at the drainage channels almost all at once, so the channels’ capacity can no longer hold the rapidly rising discharge. The phenomenon is clearly visible in big cities like Jakarta and Bekasi,” he explained. 
 Areas like that, he continued, also have a relatively shallow water table, so the soil reaches saturation faster when rain lasts a long time. Once all the soil’s pore space is filled with water, the next rain can no longer soak in and immediately forms standing water on the surface. 
 For that reason, efforts are needed to return some rainwater to the ground from the moment it first lands on the surface. Yuli said infiltration well is the answer, one water conservation technology that can be applied starting at the household scale is the infiltration well. 
 Infiltration Wells Reduce Runoff
 Yuli explained that, put simply, the well is built in a circular or rectangular shape to a certain depth. Rainwater that enters is not directly discharged into the drainage channel, but slowly soaks through the soil layers until it reaches the shallow aquifer. 
 “The concept is not to get rid of water as fast as possible, but to return rainwater to where it came from, which is the soil,” Yuli said. 
 This principle is what separates the conventional drainage approach from the environmentally minded drainage concept, or eco-drainage. Whereas drainage systems have so far been designed to speed up water flow toward rivers, infiltration wells slow the movement of water so the peak flood discharge can be reduced. 
 The benefits don’t stop at reducing standing water in the rainy season. Water that manages to soak in becomes a groundwater reserve that is reusable when the dry season arrives. This process helps maintain the water table so residents’ wells keep a water supply. 
 “In coastal areas, infiltration wells also help maintain groundwater pressure, which can reduce the risk of land subsidence and slow seawater intrusion onto land,” he added. 
 The soil also works naturally as a filter. Yuli explained, “When rainwater passes through the soil layers, certain particles are filtered out before it finally joins the aquifer system.” 
 Even so, Yuli cautioned that not every location is suitable for an infiltration well. Its effectiveness depends heavily on local hydrogeological conditions. 
 Sandy or gravelly soil with good permeability is more ideal than clay soil, which tends to be impermeable. The bottom of the well must also sit above the water table so there is still room for infiltration. 
 Infiltration wells also must not be built too close to septic tanks, clean-water wells, or building foundations. The water fed in should also come from rainwater that has passed through a sediment settling tank so the soil pores don’t clog quickly. 
 “Building an infiltration well must take into account soil conditions, the depth of the water table, and the quality of the water to be infiltrated. With proper planning, these wells can still be built at the household scale,” he stressed. 
 In addition, he said, climate change makes infiltration wells increasingly relevant. Rain patterns now tend to be more extreme: high-intensity rain in a short time. Water arrives far faster than the soil can absorb it. 
 As a result, people face two problems at once. In the rainy season, runoff triggers floods and standing water. Conversely, when the dry season comes, groundwater reserves thin out because little water had the chance to soak in. 
 A long-term solution isn’t just widening drainage channels or speeding water toward rivers. Cities also need to restore the function of infiltration areas through various green infrastructure, including infiltration wells. 
 Some regions have proven the benefits of this approach. In the Special Region of Yogyakarta (DIY), for example, building infiltration wells is encouraged through regulation and community movements to maintain groundwater availability while reducing the potential for standing water in urban areas. 
 Citing a press release from the Audit Board of Indonesia (BPK) DIY Representative Office, Head of the Water Resources and Drainage Division at the DIY Public Works, Housing, Energy, and Mineral Resources Agency (PUPESDM), Subarja, said that building infiltration wells and bore wells is supported through special privileges funds (danais) in the Water Resources and Drainage sector. The program targets Special Strategic Space (SRS) areas under the special privileges affairs on spatial planning, with construction sites in Gunungkidul, Kulon Progo, and Bantul Regencies. 
 These efforts show that rainwater management is not only an issue when floods occur, but also part of a strategy to keep water resources sustainable over the long term. 
 For Yuli, facing the flood threat needs to start with a change in how we view rainwater. Rainwater is not merely runoff to be channeled out of residential areas right away, but a resource to be managed and returned to the soil. 
 “Rainwater is not an enemy to be thrown away quickly. On the contrary, it is a resource that must be returned to the soil so the hydrological cycle stays intact,” he concluded.
